**Two aircraft carry the designation X-44A, both of them Lockheed Martin, and only one of them was ever built.** The famous one is the Multi-Axis No-Tail Aircraft, a proposed derivative of the F-22 with every tail surface deleted and every axis of control handed to the exhaust, which was approved in 1999, funded briefly and cancelled without metal being cut [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]]. The other was a tailless unmanned flying wing of about nine metres span, built by the Skunk Works in 1999, first flown in 2001, and kept out of public view until March 2018 [[Skunk Works reveals the missing link in a secret unmanned history][ref_flightglobal_x44a]]. **The aeroplane that exists is the one nobody had heard of, and it is now in a museum** [[Lockheed Martin X-44A, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x44a_museum]].
This is the forty-fifth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the **This is a documentation-poor article and the section order is the full one.** The genre note in this series recognises four classes and sets the test for choosing between them, which is whether a vehicle existed and produced data rather than whether the designation is disputed. **A vehicle existed and produced data, and almost none of that data has been released.** No specifications for the X-44A have ever been published beyond a span, an engine and two dates, and the MANTA never reached the point of having specifications to publish. So the sections below are the same sections a documented aircraft gets, and **the statement of what is unknown carries the weight a specification table would otherwise carry.**

**The finding is that the question the MANTA existed to answer had already been answered in flight, five years earlier, by an aeroplane this series has already covered.** The X-31 flew a hundred percent simulated vertical tail removal at Mach 1.2 and 37,500 feet in March 1994, restabilised by yaw thrust vectoring, and its report concludes that tailless and reduced-tail fighters are feasible [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]] [[Huber and Schellenger 1994][research_huberpeter_schellengerharveyg_1994]]. **The interesting question is therefore not whether the MANTA would have worked but what its demonstration point was worth**, and that turns out to be arithmetic rather than opinion. The demonstration was flown within fourteen percent of the worst Mach number in the entire supersonic envelope, so it very nearly covered everything above the speed of sound. **What it did not cover is the landing**, and the reason is the throttle rather than the aerodynamics.

## The Research Question

**The binding unknown was whether an aeroplane can be held straight by its engines when it has nothing else to be held straight by.**

A vertical tail exists to supply two different things that are easy to confuse. It supplies **static directional stability**, meaning a restoring moment that grows with sideslip and points the nose back into the wind, and it supplies **control power**, meaning a moment the pilot can command at will. **Deleting the tail removes both, and the two are replaced by different mechanisms.** Stability is replaced by feedback, which is a matter of sensors, computation and actuator bandwidth. Control power is replaced by thrust deflection, which is a matter of how much momentum flows through the nozzle and how far that nozzle sits behind the centre of gravity. **The distinction between the two is standard and is made in every treatment of the subject** [[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin_reid]] [[Nelson, Flight stability and automatic control][book_nelson]] [[Perkins and Hage, Airplane performance, stability and control][book_perkins_hage]], and the conventional way of sizing the surface that supplies both is a tail volume coefficient, which is a ratio of areas and arms carrying no propulsion term at all [[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]] [[Torenbeek, Synthesis of subsonic airplane design][book_torenbeek]]. **A thrust-vectored aeroplane has no tail volume, so none of that apparatus applies to it**, which is the reason this article builds the comparison from first principles rather than from a design handbook.

**The reason to delete it is not aerodynamic elegance.** A vertical tail is the single largest contributor to the radar cross section of an otherwise carefully shaped aeroplane, because a flat surface standing perpendicular to the wing is a corner reflector for every illumination in the horizontal plane, and the shaping literature has said so for as long as it has existed [[Knott, Shaeffer and Tuley, Radar cross section][book_knott]]. It also carries a trim drag penalty, a weight penalty, an actuation penalty and, on a supersonic aeroplane, a wave drag penalty. **The MANTA's own advertised benefits were reduced mechanical complexity, greater internal fuel volume and greater agility** [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]] [[X-44 MANTA Multi-Axis No-Tail Aircraft, GlobalSecurity][ref_globalsecurity_x44]], which is a list of four different disciplines each wanting the same part removed.

**The question this article asks is narrower and answerable.** Given that the X-31 demonstrated tailless control at one flight condition, **what fraction of a fighter's envelope does one demonstrated point actually cover?** That question has a closed-form answer that needs no wing area, no yaw derivative and no moment arm, and it is the spine of everything below.

**For the unmanned aircraft the question is different, because the vehicle is subsonic and has no vertical tail to argue about.** There the binding unknown was whether a small tailless flying wing could be designed, built and flown quickly enough to matter, and the article treats that as a manufacturing question rather than an aerodynamic one, because that is how its own programme described it [[Skunk Works reveals the tailless X-44A][ref_uasvision_x44a]].

## Programme Origin

### The MANTA, and the Aircraft It Was to Be Made From

**The MANTA was a conversion proposal and not a clean-sheet aeroplane.** The design took the F-22's fuselage and engines, replaced the wing with a stretched delta, and deleted the vertical and horizontal tails entirely, leaving attitude control to three-axis thrust vectoring [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]] [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA tailless technology demonstrator proposal][ref_militaryfactory_x44]]. Preliminary work was under way by May 1999. **The National Aeronautics and Space Administration approved the programme to start in June 1999 and the designation recorded at that point is X-44A.** Funding ended in 2000.

**The sources disagree about the end date and the article does not resolve the disagreement.** The encyclopaedia entry says funding ended in 2000 [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]]. Later secondary accounts place the cancellation in 2001 and attribute it to shifting priorities. **Neither account cites a programme document**, and this article treats the year as unsettled rather than choosing between two uncited claims.

**Nothing was built.** There is no airframe, no wind tunnel entry that has been released under the name, no flight and no report. The MANTA is a set of drawings and a set of claims, and the claims are what can be tested.

### The X-44A, and the Programme That Had Gone Quiet

**The unmanned X-44A fills a hole in a public record that had been visibly empty.** Lockheed's high-altitude unmanned reconnaissance line ran from the RQ-3 DarkStar, which first flew on 29 March 1996 and was terminated by the Department of Defense in January 1999 [[Lockheed Martin RQ-3 DarkStar][ref_darkstar_wikipedia]], to the P-175 Polecat, which first flew in 2005 [[Lockheed Martin P-175 Polecat][ref_polecat_wikipedia]], to the RQ-170 Sentinel [[Lockheed Martin RQ-170 Sentinel][ref_rq170_wikipedia]]. **Between January 1999 and 2005 the public record showed nothing at all.** That the gap existed at all is a property of how the organisation works rather than an accident, since the Skunk Works was built to run programmes that do not announce themselves [[Rich and Janos, Skunk Works][book_rich_janos]]. The X-44A occupies exactly that gap, having been built in 1999, the year DarkStar was cancelled, and flown in 2001 [[Skunk Works reveals the missing link in a secret unmanned history][ref_flightglobal_x44a]].

**Its stated purposes were manufacturing and configuration, not performance.** The programme is described as proving rapid manufacturing techniques, demonstrating penetrating reconnaissance, and establishing the aerodynamic validity of a relatively small tailless swept flying wing [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]]. **That ordering matters**, because a vehicle built to prove that it can be built quickly is dimensioned by its factory rather than by its mission, and the derivation later in this article finds a wing loading consistent with that reading and not with an endurance optimum.

**It was revealed at the Los Angeles County Air Show in March 2018 and placed on public display in October 2020**, in the Research and Development gallery of the National Museum of the United States Air Force [[Lockheed Martin X-44A, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x44a_museum]] [[Exclusive photos, the X-44A breaks cover][ref_twz_x44a_photos]]. **Seventeen years elapsed between the first flight and the first photograph.**

## The Designation and Its Two Referents

**This is the fourth article in the last six to turn on a designation that may not belong to the vehicle it is attached to, and it is the first in which both claimants are the same company.**

The pattern to date is worth stating because it is now long enough to be a property of the system rather than a run of coincidences. The [X-39][related_post_a336_x39_reserved_never_assigned] was reserved and never assigned to anything. The [X-41][related_post_a338_x41_common_aero_vehicle] carried a designation allocated years before the programme it is now attached to existed. The [X-42][related_post_a339_orbital_sciences_x42] had two sources describing different vehicles four years apart, one official and never used, one unofficial and actually used. The [X-40][related_post_a337_boeing_x40] and the [X-43][related_post_a340_micro_craft_x43] are the two exceptions in the run, both undisputed, which is why the count above is four of six rather than six of six. **The X-44 is the sharpest case, because both vehicles are Lockheed Martin products, both were current in 1999, and both are recorded as X-44A.**

**Three things about the record are worth stating precisely.**

**First, the reference literature has split into two entries instead of reconciling them.** The general encyclopaedia carries a page for the MANTA and a separate page for the unmanned vehicle, and the second page states that it is apparently unrelated to the first [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]] [[Lockheed Martin X-44, the unmanned vehicle][ref_x44_uav_wikipedia]]. A disambiguation page exists to route between them [[X44, the disambiguation page][ref_x44_disambiguation]]. **Splitting is the correct editorial response to a genuine collision and it is not a resolution of one.**

**Second, the specialist designation registry does not carry the number at all.** Andreas Parsch's Appendix 4 to the Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles covers undesignated and unusual unmanned vehicles and holds pages for the X-41, the X-42, the X-45, the X-47 and the X-48 [[Parsch, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles, Appendix 4][ref_parsch_app4]]. **A request for an X-44 page returns a not-found response listing those five as near misses.** The registry that documents this series' other disputed numbers most carefully has nothing to say about this one. That is an absence rather than a denial, and this article reports it as an absence.

**Third, the journalism that broke the story said openly that it did not know.** The account that first published photographs states that it is unclear how the flying wing came to carry the same designation as the manned proposal and that there appears to be no direct relation between the two programmes [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]]. **A reporter who has the aeroplane and the photographs and still cannot explain the number is evidence about the number, not about the reporting.**

**The designation system has a documented allocation process and it is not silent about duplication.** Aircraft designations are governed by Department of the Air Force Instruction 16-401, which covers the naming of aerospace vehicles and the bureaucratic steps by which a designation is actually assigned [[Parsch, Current Designations of U.S. Military Aircraft][ref_parsch_aircraft]]. **A number issued twice is therefore either a failure of that process or evidence that one of the two allocations was never made through it.** The public record does not say which, and this article does not guess.

**One structural observation survives without resolving anything.** The X-planes numbering is a finite resource issued consecutively and never replenished, which is the mechanism the [X-39 article][related_post_a336_x39_reserved_never_assigned] rests its permanence argument on. **A number spent twice is a number spent once as far as the sequence is concerned**, and the sequence carries no record of the collision. The cost of the ambiguity is borne entirely by readers of the record and not at all by the register.

## Sizing From First Principles

**The MANTA's claim is testable without knowing anything about the MANTA.** What follows derives the quantity that decides whether propulsive yaw control is sufficient, shows that two of the three variables it appears to depend on cancel identically, and then locates the flight condition that binds.

### The Quantity That Has to Be Compared

**A tailless aeroplane needs a yawing moment and has one available. The question is the ratio.**

Let $q$ be the dynamic pressure, $S$ the wing reference area, $b$ the span, $C_{n\beta}$ the directional stability derivative and $\beta$ the sideslip angle. The aerodynamic yawing moment that must be produced, whether to trim a disturbance or to restrain a divergence, is

$$N_{\text{req}} = q S b \left| C_{n\beta} \right| \beta$$

Let $F_{g}$ be the gross thrust passing through the nozzles, $\ell$ the distance from the centre of gravity to the nozzle exit and $\delta$ the yaw deflection angle of the jet. The moment available is

$$N_{\text{av}} = F_{g} \ell \sin \delta$$

**The whole argument is the ratio of these two, and it is worth naming.**

$$\mathcal{R} \equiv \frac{N_{\text{av}}}{N_{\text{req}}} = \frac{F_{g} \ell \sin \delta}{q S b \left| C_{n\beta} \right| \beta}$$

**Dynamic pressure is not an independent quantity and writing it in terms of static pressure is the step that makes everything else work.** With $\gamma$ the ratio of specific heats, $p$ the ambient static pressure and $M$ the Mach number,

$$q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho M^{2} \gamma R T = \tfrac{1}{2} \gamma p M^{2} = 0.7 \, p M^{2}$$

The moment form above is the standard linearised one [[Yechout and Morris, Introduction to aircraft flight mechanics][book_yechout]] [[Schmidt, Modern flight dynamics][book_schmidt]] [[Roskam, Airplane flight dynamics and automatic flight controls][book_roskam]], and the substitution for dynamic pressure follows from the definition of Mach number and the perfect gas law together [[Anderson, Fundamentals of aerodynamics][book_anderson]] [[McCormick, Aerodynamics, aeronautics and flight mechanics][book_mccormick]]. **That is an identity and not an approximation.** It is verified in the accompanying computation by evaluating both forms at every flight condition used in this article and requiring agreement to within one part in a million.

### The Engine Puts the Static Pressure Back In

**Gross thrust is not a constant and the way it varies is what produces the result.** A fixed-geometry engine running at its maximum corrected rotational speed passes a constant corrected mass flow, so the physical mass flow follows the total conditions at the compressor face. With $\delta_{2}$ and $\theta_{2}$ the total pressure and total temperature at that station referred to sea level static conditions,

$$\dot{m} = \dot{m}_{\text{ref}} \frac{\delta_{2}}{\sqrt{\theta_{2}}}$$

**This is the corrected-parameter machinery of engine performance and it is not specific to this problem** [[Mattingly, Elements of gas turbine propulsion][book_mattingly_propulsion]] [[Cumpsty, Jet propulsion][book_cumpsty]]. It is used here for the one property that matters, which is how physical mass flow varies when ambient conditions change.

The total conditions follow from the ambient conditions and the flight Mach number through the isentropic relations, reduced by the inlet total pressure recovery $\eta_{r}$,

$$\delta_{2} = \frac{p}{p_{\text{SL}}} \left( 1 + \tfrac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}} \eta_{r}
\qquad
\theta_{2} = \frac{T}{T_{\text{SL}}} \left( 1 + \tfrac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)$$

which for $\gamma = 1.4$ gives, after cancelling one half power of the ram term,

$$\dot{m} \propto \frac{p}{p_{\text{SL}}} \, \eta_{r} \, \frac{\left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3}}{\sqrt{T / T_{\text{SL}}}}$$

**Gross thrust is that mass flow times a jet velocity.** The jet velocity of an engine running at its afterburner temperature limit through a nozzle that is choked and well above its critical pressure ratio is nearly constant across the flight envelope, and this article treats it as constant and carries the consequence in the epistemic state.

$$F_{g} = \dot{m} V_{j} + \left( p_{e} - p \right) A_{e} \approx \dot{m} V_{j}$$

### The Static Pressure Cancels Exactly

**Assembling the ratio, the ambient static pressure appears once in the numerator and once in the denominator, to the same power.**

$$\mathcal{R} \propto \frac{ \dfrac{p}{p_{\text{SL}}} \eta_{r} \dfrac{(1 + 0.2 M^{2})^{3}}{\sqrt{T/T_{\text{SL}}}} }{ 0.7 \, p M^{2} }
= \frac{ \eta_{r} \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3} }{ 0.7 \, p_{\text{SL}} \, M^{2} \sqrt{T/T_{\text{SL}}} }$$

**The pressure is gone, so the ratio does not depend on altitude except through temperature.** Above the tropopause the standard atmosphere holds temperature constant at 216.65 kelvin, so in that region **the ratio is a function of Mach number alone.**

$$\mathcal{R}(M) \propto \frac{\eta_{r}(M) \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3}}{M^{2}} \qquad h > 11 \ \text{km}$$

**This is checked rather than asserted.** The accompanying computation evaluates the ratio through the full standard atmosphere at Mach 1.2 at five altitudes from 11,000 metres to 65,000 feet and requires the results to agree to within one part in ten to the twelfth. They do. It then compares the atmosphere-driven computation against the closed form above at three further altitudes and requires exact agreement. **The cancellation is structural and is not a numerical coincidence.**

**Below the tropopause the cancellation is only partial, because temperature varies there.** The residue is not negligible and it runs the unhelpful way.

| altitude | ratio relative to 11 km, same Mach |
|---|---|
| sea level | 0.8671 |
| 10,000 ft | 0.8985 |
| 20,000 ft | 0.9337 |
| 30,000 ft | 0.9733 |
| 11 km and above | 1.0000 |

**A tailless aeroplane is thirteen percent worse off at sea level than at altitude at the same Mach number**, and the entire effect is the temperature term $\sqrt{T/T_{\text{SL}}}$, which enters because a colder engine face passes more mass.

### The Ratio Has a Minimum and It Is Not Where Intuition Puts It

**Intuition says the hardest case for a thrust-vectored aeroplane is the fastest one, because dynamic pressure grows as the square of Mach number. Intuition is wrong, because ram compression grows faster.**

Taking ideal recovery for a moment, the Mach dependence is

$$f(M) = \frac{\left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3}}{M^{2}}$$

Differentiating with respect to $u = M^{2}$,

$$\frac{d}{du} \left[ \frac{(1 + 0.2u)^{3}}{u} \right] = \frac{(1 + 0.2u)^{2} \left( 0.4 u - 1 \right)}{u^{2}}$$

**which vanishes at $u = 2.5$, so the worst Mach number is exactly $\sqrt{5/2}$.**

$$M^{\ast} = \sqrt{2.5} = 1.5811 \qquad f(M^{\ast}) = \frac{1.5^{3}}{2.5} = \frac{3.375}{2.5} = 1.35$$

**Both the location and the value are exact and both are verified independently.** The computation finds the same minimising Mach number by bisection on a numerically differenced derivative, agreeing to six decimal places, and asserts the value 1.35 to machine precision. **A closed form that lands on a round number is usually a mistake, so it was checked rather than admired.**

**Adding a realistic inlet total pressure recovery moves the minimum and does not remove it.** Using the military specification correlation, $\eta_{r} = 1 - 0.075 (M-1)^{1.35}$ above Mach one and unity below,

| Mach | ideal recovery | with recovery |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 7.900 | 7.968 |
| 0.5 | 3.121 | 3.148 |
| 0.7 | 1.821 | 1.836 |
| 0.9 | 1.305 | 1.317 |
| 1.0 | 1.165 | 1.175 |
| 1.2 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| 1.4 | 0.927 | 0.915 |
| 1.5811 | 0.910 | 0.885 |
| 1.674 | 0.913 | 0.881 |
| 1.8 | 0.931 | 0.887 |
| 2.0 | 0.983 | 0.917 |
| 2.25 | 1.085 | 0.984 |

**Every column is normalised to Mach 1.2, which is the condition the X-31 actually flew.** With recovery included the minimum sits at Mach 1.674 and the demonstrated point stands 1.135 times above it.

**That number is the answer to the question this article set.** The X-31 demonstrated tailless control at a point that is **thirteen and a half percent easier than the worst point in the supersonic envelope**, and no point between Mach 1.2 and Mach 2.25 is more than thirteen and a half percent harder than what was flown. **A single demonstrated supersonic point very nearly covered the whole supersonic envelope**, which is a far stronger result than the demonstration claimed for itself, and it follows from a cancellation rather than from a simulation.

**It also inverts the expectation.** The demonstration was not flown at a soft condition chosen to flatter the concept. **On this measure it was flown next to the hardest one available**, and whether that was by design or by the accident of what the X-31's envelope allowed, the public record does not say.

### The Crosswind Identity, in Which the Temperature Cancels Too

**The comparison above holds the sideslip angle fixed, which is right for a manoeuvre and wrong for a wind.** A crosswind, or a lateral gust, has a fixed speed rather than a fixed angle, and the angle it produces grows as the aeroplane slows. With $V_{c}$ the crosswind speed,

$$\beta = \arctan \frac{V_{c}}{V} \approx \frac{V_{c}}{V} = \frac{V_{c}}{M \sqrt{\gamma R T}}$$

Substituting into the required moment,

$$N_{\text{req}} \propto q \beta = 0.7 \, p M^{2} \cdot \frac{V_{c}}{M \sqrt{\gamma R T}} \propto \frac{p M}{\sqrt{T}}$$

**and the available moment already carries the same pressure and the same square root of temperature.**

$$N_{\text{av}} \propto \frac{p \, \eta_{r} \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3}}{\sqrt{T}}$$

**Both cancel. The required vector angle for a crosswind of given speed depends on Mach number and on nothing else whatever.**

$$\frac{N_{\text{req}}}{N_{\text{av}}} \propto \frac{M}{\eta_{r}(M) \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3}}$$

**No pressure, no temperature, no altitude, no density and no true airspeed.** The computation checks this at Mach 0.8 across five altitudes from sea level to 55,000 feet with the throttle held, and the results agree to better than four parts in ten thousand, the residue being the difference between the arctangent and its argument.

**Differentiating gives a result cleaner than the last one.**

$$\frac{d}{dM} \left[ M \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{-3} \right] = \frac{1 - M^{2}}{\left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{4}}$$

**The crosswind demand peaks at exactly Mach one**, at every altitude, in every atmosphere, for every crosswind speed and for every aeroplane. The maximum value of the ideal form is $1/1.728$.

| Mach | crosswind demand, Mach one taken as unity |
|---|---|
| 0.23 | 0.385 |
| 0.4 | 0.629 |
| 0.6 | 0.842 |
| 0.8 | 0.963 |
| 1.0 | 1.000 |
| 1.2 | 0.971 |
| 1.5 | 0.850 |
| 1.8 | 0.695 |
| 2.25 | 0.477 |

**Read at equal throttle, that table says the approach is the easiest case in the envelope and not the hardest.** At an approach Mach number of 0.227 the demand is 38.5 percent of the transonic peak. **This is the opposite of what the design of every conventional aeroplane suggests**, because a conventional fin's authority falls with dynamic pressure while a nozzle's does not.

### The Throttle Is What Binds, and It Binds Hard

**The table above holds the throttle fixed, and on an approach the throttle is not fixed. It is nearly closed.**

An aeroplane descending a three degree glide slope at a lift to drag ratio of six in the landing configuration needs a thrust of

$$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{1}{L/D} - \sin \gamma = \frac{1}{6} - \sin 3^{\circ} = 0.16667 - 0.05234 = 0.11433$$

which for a landing weight near twenty tonnes against two engines of 156 kilonewtons each is about **7.2 percent of the maximum available thrust.** **The control authority falls with it, because the control authority is the thrust.**

**Inverting for the throttle setting that restores the demonstrated margin gives the size of the problem.** Taking the X-31's Mach 1.2 point at maximum thrust as the unit of adequacy, and requiring the same ratio of required to available moment on a sea-level approach at 150 knots in a 15 metre per second crosswind, the throttle must stand at

$$\text{throttle} = 0.384 \qquad \text{against } 0.072 \text{ needed to fly the glide slope}$$

**a factor of 5.33.** **The aeroplane must carry more than five times the thrust its flight path needs, purely in order to have the yaw control its flight path does not need until something goes wrong.**

**That requirement is not merely expensive. It is impossible, and saying why is the strongest result in this article.** An aeroplane in level flight at a given thrust has a lift to drag ratio fixed by that thrust and its weight. At 38.4 percent of maximum thrust, the implied ratio is

| landing weight | implied lift to drag ratio at that thrust |
|---|---|
| 20,000 kg | 1.59 |
| 22,000 kg | 1.75 |
| 24,000 kg | 1.91 |

**No aeroplane approaches at a lift to drag ratio below two.** A fighter with gear and flaps down is near six. **To absorb the thrust that pure propulsive yaw control demands on approach, the aeroplane would have to be three times draggier than a fighter in the landing configuration is**, and there is no drag device on a stealth aeroplane that can do that without undoing the reason the tails were removed in the first place.

**The conclusion follows without any unpublished number.** Every airframe quantity cancelled in the ratio, so the wing area, the span, the yaw derivative and the moment arm never had to be known. **Pure thrust vectoring cannot meet a crosswind landing requirement, and a tailless fighter therefore needs an aerodynamic yaw effector that works at low speed even though it does not need one supersonically.** That is exactly the architecture the [X-36][related_post_a333_mcdonnell_douglas_x36] flew, with split ailerons acting as drag rudders alongside its vectoring nozzle, and the [X-31][related_post_a328_rockwell_mbb_x31] investigated, with differential canard deflection studied as a yaw generator of the same order as its thrust vectoring vanes [[Whiting 1996][research_whitingmatthewrobert_1996]].

**The MANTA proposed to delete every aerodynamic surface. On this arithmetic, that specific claim does not survive contact with a crosswind.**

### The Engine-Out Case, in Which the Thrust Cancels

**The classic reason a twin-engine aeroplane has a large fin is the failure of one engine, and for a thrust-vectored aeroplane that case is almost free.** The reason is an identity.

Let the live engine sit a lateral distance $y$ from the centreline with its nozzle a distance $\ell$ aft of the centre of gravity, and let it be deflected through an angle $\delta$. Its axial component produces a yawing moment about the centre of gravity of $F_{g} y \cos \delta$ toward the dead side, and its lateral component produces $F_{g} \ell \sin \delta$ the other way. Setting them equal,

$$F_{g} \ell \sin \delta = F_{g} y \cos \delta \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \tan \delta = \frac{y}{\ell}$$

**The thrust cancels identically.** The vector angle needed to trim an engine failure depends on nothing but where the engines are. It does not depend on how much thrust the live engine is making, on altitude, on speed, on the atmosphere or on any aerodynamic property of the aeroplane whatever.

**This is verified by solving the moment balance numerically without cancelling the thrust by hand**, at thrusts spanning four orders of magnitude from one kilonewton to one meganewton, and requiring the root to agree with the arctangent to within one part in a billion. It does.

| lateral offset $y$ | arm $\ell$ | required $\delta$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.70 m | 6.5 m | 6.15 deg |
| 0.70 m | 8.5 m | 4.71 deg |
| 0.85 m | 7.5 m | 6.47 deg |
| 1.00 m | 6.5 m | 8.75 deg |
| 1.00 m | 7.5 m | 7.59 deg |
| 1.20 m | 6.5 m | 10.46 deg |
| 1.20 m | 8.5 m | 8.04 deg |

**The published nozzle deflection of the F-22 is twenty degrees, and the whole of that table is inside eleven.** Adding the windmilling drag of the dead engine at ten percent of the live engine's gross thrust takes the middle case from 7.59 degrees to 8.34, which is still comfortably inside.

**The reason a fin is large and a nozzle need not be is worth stating plainly.** A fin must be sized for the engine-out case at the lowest speed at which it can occur, because the fin's authority falls as the square of the speed while the thrust asymmetry does not fall at all. **A nozzle's authority and the asymmetry it must cancel are the same quantity**, so the case is speed-independent by construction. **The engine-out requirement, which is one of the two classic fin-sizing cases, simply does not size a thrust-vectored aeroplane.**

**The other classic case is the crosswind landing, and that is the one the previous section showed cannot be met.** Two sizing cases, opposite answers, and the article would have got both wrong by reasoning from the fin.

### The Divergence Is Too Fast for a Person

**Control authority is necessary and not sufficient. An unstable aeroplane must also be stabilised faster than it diverges.**

With the tail removed the directional mode is a divergence and not an oscillation, and its growth rate follows from the yawing moment of inertia $I_{z}$.

$$\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{q S b \left| C_{n\beta} \right|}{I_{z}}} \qquad t_{2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

**Neither the yaw derivative of a tailless F-22 nor its yawing inertia has been published**, so the table brackets both across their plausible ranges rather than asserting a value.

| $\left|C_{n\beta}\right|$ per radian | $I_{z}$ kg m² | $t_{2}$ approach | $t_{2}$ Mach 1.2 at 37,500 ft |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.03 | 1.2 × 10⁵ | 0.706 s | 0.292 s |
| 0.03 | 2.0 × 10⁵ | 0.911 s | 0.377 s |
| 0.06 | 1.6 × 10⁵ | 0.576 s | 0.238 s |
| 0.10 | 1.2 × 10⁵ | 0.386 s | 0.160 s |
| 0.10 | 2.0 × 10⁵ | 0.499 s | 0.206 s |

**Every cell in that table is inside one second, and the whole supersonic column is inside four tenths.** A trained pilot's reaction time to an unexpected disturbance is not inside four tenths of a second, and no part of the bracket makes it so. **The stabilisation loop is therefore machinery rather than a person, and that conclusion follows from arithmetic and not from preference.**

**This is why the X-31 report emphasises sensors.** Its stated lessons concern sensor-related issues and their importance to controlling a directionally unstable vehicle [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]], which is exactly what the table predicts. **When the loop must close in a fraction of a second, the limiting component is the thing that measures sideslip, not the thing that produces the moment.**

### The X-44A, Derived From Its Mission Because Nothing Else Is Published

**One dimension, one engine and two dates are the entire released specification.** The span is about 30 feet, or 9.14 metres. The engine is a Williams F112 of 732 pounds force, which is 3,256 newtons [[Williams F112][ref_f112_wikipedia]] [[Williams International F112-WR-100 Turbofan, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_f112_museum]]. It was built in 1999 and flown in 2001. **The engine is a cruise missile powerplant**, developed for the AGM-129 Advanced Cruise Missile [[AGM-129 Advanced Cruise Missile][ref_agm129_wikipedia]], which is a choice that buys small size and low cost and brings with it a design point nothing like an aeroplane's.

**The most useful comparison available is not to another unmanned aircraft. It is to the X-36, which used the same engine.** The [X-36][related_post_a333_mcdonnell_douglas_x36] carried an F112 rated at 700 pounds force in an airframe of 3.18 metres span and 576 kilograms maximum weight, giving a thrust to weight ratio of 0.56 [[McDonnell Douglas X-36][ref_x36_wikipedia]]. **The X-44A spans 2.87 times as much on the same thrust**, which taking wing area as proportional to the square of span is a factor of

$$\left( \frac{9.144}{3.18} \right)^{2} = 8.27$$

**more wing on the same engine.** Two aircraft with one powerplant and an eight-fold difference in wing area are not variants of a concept. They are answers to different questions, and the wing is where the difference is recorded.

**Calibrating the thrust lapse on the DarkStar puts a number on the rest.** The DarkStar published a service ceiling of 45,000 feet, a gross weight of 3,856 kilograms and a Williams FJ44-1A of 8.45 kilonewtons [[Lockheed Martin RQ-3 DarkStar][ref_darkstar_wikipedia]]. At the ceiling, thrust available equals drag at the best lift to drag ratio, so

$$T_{\text{SL}} \sigma^{n} = \frac{W}{(L/D)_{\max}} \qquad (L/D)_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\pi e A\!R}{C_{D_{0}}}}$$

The second of those follows from a parabolic drag polar and is the form every preliminary design text gives [[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]] [[Filippone, Advanced aircraft flight performance][book_filippone]], and the thrust lapse exponent is the quantity that a design text would supply from a table and that this article instead measures [[Mattingly, Aircraft engine design][book_mattingly_engine_design]].

Taking a 42 square metre wing, which gives an aspect ratio of 10.53, an Oswald efficiency of 0.85 and a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.015, the best ratio is 21.65 and the required thrust at the ceiling is 1,747 newtons. The density ratio there is 0.1936, so

$$n = \frac{\ln \left( 1751 / 8450 \right)}{\ln 0.1936} = 0.960$$

**Thrust falls with density and not with pressure, which is the wrong answer for a turbojet and the right one for a fan.** The two differ by the temperature ratio and at that altitude they differ by a third, so the distinction is not academic.

**Applying the same lapse to the F112 gives a locus and not a point, because weight and ceiling are not separately knowable.**

| assumed ceiling | density ratio | thrust available | implied weight | implied wing loading | cruise Mach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35,000 ft | 0.3099 | 1,057 N | 2,334 kg | 294 kg/m² | 0.516 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.2462 | 848 N | 1,871 kg | 236 kg/m² | 0.521 |
| 45,000 ft | 0.1936 | 673 N | 1,486 kg | 187 kg/m² | 0.523 |
| 50,000 ft | 0.1522 | 534 N | 1,180 kg | 149 kg/m² | 0.526 |
| 55,000 ft | 0.1197 | 424 N | 937 kg | 118 kg/m² | 0.528 |

**The DarkStar's own wing loading on the same assumptions is 91.8 kilograms per square metre.** At a matched ceiling of 45,000 feet the X-44A's is 187, **a factor of 2.04 higher**, and it only falls to the DarkStar's value if the aircraft is assumed to reach nearly 60,000 feet on a cruise-missile engine.

**That is a finding about what the aeroplane was for.** A high wing loading is what a designer accepts when altitude and endurance are not the objective. It is consistent with a vehicle built to demonstrate that a small tailless flying wing can be manufactured quickly and flown at all, which is what the programme said it was for [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]], and it is inconsistent with a vehicle sized to loiter. **The derivation and the stated purpose agree, which is worth more than either alone**, because the derivation used none of the words in the statement.

**One caveat is load-bearing and is stated here rather than hidden in the epistemic state.** The DarkStar's wing area is not published in the sources used and 42 square metres is an assumption. The lapse exponent is sensitive to it, and every number in the X-44A table inherits that sensitivity. **What does not inherit it is the ratio between the two wing loadings**, because the same assumed aspect ratio and the same assumed drag polar enter both, so the factor of two is far more robust than either loading is.

## Dependent Systems

### The Nozzle the F-22 Does Not Have

**The single most consequential fact about the MANTA is one that its own description obscures.** The proposal is routinely described as converting an F-22 by deleting its tails and using its thrust vectoring nozzles for control [[X-44 MANTA Multi-Axis No-Tail Aircraft, GlobalSecurity][ref_globalsecurity_x44]]. **The F-22 has no yaw vectoring.** Its Pratt and Whitney F119 engines carry two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzles that deflect through plus or minus twenty degrees **in pitch only** [[Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor][ref_f22_wikipedia]] [[Pratt and Whitney F119][ref_f119_wikipedia]].

**A two-dimensional nozzle deflects in the plane of its flaps and in no other.** Producing yaw from the same nozzle requires the sidewalls to become deflecting surfaces, which is a different piece of hardware in the same envelope rather than a different schedule for existing hardware. **The MANTA is therefore not a subtraction from the F-22. It is a subtraction and an addition, and the addition is the harder half.**

**That addition has been measured, and the measurement is encouraging.** Capone and Bare tested an advanced twin-engine supersonic-cruise fighter model with a two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzle designed to give yaw vector angles of zero, ten and twenty degrees through yaw flaps in the nozzle sidewalls, with roll obtained from differential pitch vectoring, across Mach 0.20 to 2.47 [[Capone and Bare 1987][research_caponefrancisj_bareeann_1987]]. **Their central result is that the force and moment increments produced by vectoring remain essentially constant over the whole angle of attack range at every Mach number tested**, and that pitch and yaw vectoring show very little cross-coupling. **A control effector whose authority does not vary with angle of attack is precisely what a tailless aeroplane needs**, because an aerodynamic fin's authority collapses exactly where a fighter most wants it.

**The wider measurement literature says the same thing across several configurations** [[Capone and Mason 1986][research_caponefj_masonml_1986]] [[Berrier 1988][research_berrierbobbyl_1988]], and the flight literature adds that vectoring hardware survives being flown [[Anna and Kidman 1994][research_annapauld_kidmandavids_1994]].

### The Wing

**The MANTA's wing is described only as a stretched delta of greater area than the F-22's, carrying more internal fuel** [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]]. No area, no sweep, no aerofoil and no aspect ratio have been released, so nothing can be dimensioned from it. **What can be said is what the change buys and what it costs.**

A larger delta buys fuel volume, which grows faster than area, and it buys a lower wing loading at fixed weight, which buys sustained turn rate at altitude. **It costs wave drag and it costs directional stability**, because a larger wing raises the destabilising contribution of the forward fuselage relative to nothing at all, and there is no longer a fin to overcome it. The tailless delta literature is unusually old and unusually direct about the second point [[White and Innis 1959][research_whitemauriced_innisrobertc_1959]] [[Smith 1953][research_smithwg_1953]] [[Harper and Jones 1947][research_harpercharlesw_jonesarthurl_1947]].

**The X-44A's wing is described in the journalism and not in any specification.** It is reported as a deep wing with pronounced inverse camber, complex curvature and a low-observable indented trailing edge, mated to a spheroidal fuselage, with modular wings [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]] [[Skunk Works reveals the tailless X-44A][ref_uasvision_x44a]]. **Modularity is the detail worth keeping**, because interchangeable wings on a demonstrator is a statement that the wing was the variable under test.

### Structure and the Manufacturing Claim

**The X-44A is reported as built from nano-carbon fibre and as a demonstration of rapid manufacturing** [[Lockheed Martin X-44, the unmanned vehicle][ref_x44_uav_wikipedia]] [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]]. **No mass fraction, no lay-up, no cure cycle and no tooling description has been released**, so the claim cannot be checked in the way the aerodynamic claims can. This article records it as a stated programme objective and not as a measured outcome.

**One thing about it is checkable and it is the timeline.** DarkStar was terminated in January 1999 and the X-44A was built in 1999. **A complete airframe inside a calendar year is itself the evidence for the manufacturing claim**, and it is the only evidence in the public record that bears on it at all.

### Sensing, Which the Flight Experiment Named as the Hard Part

**The divergence table above says the loop must close in a fraction of a second, and the X-31 report says what that costs.** Its lessons concern sensor-related issues and their importance both to simulating a tailless configuration and to controlling a directionally unstable one [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]]. **Sideslip is the hardest air data quantity to measure well.** It is small, it is measured at a boom or a port in a flow field that the aeroplane itself distorts, and on a stealth aeroplane the obvious instrument is a protrusion of exactly the kind the configuration exists to avoid.

**This is the sharpest unstated tension in the MANTA concept.** The aeroplane deletes its fin to reduce its radar cross section, and the deletion creates a hard requirement for a fast, accurate measurement of the very quantity that a low-observable nose is worst at supplying. **The public record does not say how the MANTA proposed to resolve that**, and the absence is recorded here rather than filled.

## The Flight Test Record

**Three flight records bear on this article and only one of them belongs to an aeroplane called X-44.**

### What the X-31 Flew

**The quasi-tailless experiment is the substantive flight record for the MANTA's question.** The technique was to use the rudder to cancel the stabilising effect of the vertical tail, and then to restabilise and control the aeroplane with yaw thrust vector commands, which gives a real aeroplane behaving like a tailless one without building a tailless one, and which was possible only because the aeroplane already carried thrust vectoring paddles for a different purpose [[Rockwell-MBB X-31][ref_x31_wikipedia]] [[Huber and Schellenger 1994][research_huberpeter_schellengerharveyg_1994]] [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]]. **The series began in March 1994.** The demonstration condition was Mach 1.2 at 37,500 feet with a simulated one hundred percent vertical tail reduction, and the manoeuvres flown were doublets, bank-to-bank rolls and wind-up turns. The quasi-tailless mode was also flown subsonically in precision approaches and ground attack profiles.

**Its conclusion is unambiguous and is quoted here because the wording matters.** Flight test and supporting simulation demonstrated that the quasi-tailless approach is effective in representing the reduced stability of tailless configurations, and that thrust vectoring could be effectively used to stabilise a directionally unstable configuration and provide control power for manoeuvre coordination. Tailless and reduced-tail fighter aircraft are, in the report's word, **definitely feasible**, with the qualification that the capability must be designed in from the beginning [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]].

**That qualification is the whole of the MANTA's difficulty in one clause.** The MANTA was a conversion.

**One thing the demonstration did not do was fly a crosswind approach on vectoring alone**, and the arithmetic above says why it could not have.

### What the X-44A Flew

**It flew in 2001 and that is the entire released flight record.** The number of flights is unknown. The dates are unknown. The envelope is unknown. No incident, no achievement and no measurement has been released. **The aeroplane survived**, which is inferable from its presence in a museum and from nothing else.

**Reporting that as a record rather than as an omission is the point of the documentation-poor class.** A vehicle that flew and produced data whose data remains classified is a different epistemic object from a vehicle that never flew, and this series has now written both.

### What the MANTA Flew

**Nothing.** No airframe was built. The programme ended with funding, not with a flight or a failure.

## What the Data Changed

**The three lines diverge sharply here and the divergence is instructive.**

**The X-31's quasi-tailless result entered the tailless design literature and stayed there.** It is the flight validation that subsequent tailless control work refers back to, and the innovative control effector programmes of the later 1990s proceed on the assumption it established [[Montgomery and Scott 1998][research_montgomeryraymondc_scottmichaela_1998]]. **A result that makes a whole line of work possible without being cited by name in every paper is easy to undervalue.**

**The X-44A's line is visible in hardware.** It sits between the DarkStar and the Polecat, and the configuration family it belongs to, being a small tailless flying wing with a low-observable planform, is the family the Polecat and the RQ-170 belong to rather than the family the DarkStar belonged to [[Skunk Works reveals the tailless X-44A][ref_uasvision_x44a]]. **The published assessment is that it belongs with the mid-2000s designs rather than the 1990s ones despite being built in 1999**, which is a claim that a demonstrator can be ahead of its own programme.

**The MANTA changed nothing that can be demonstrated.** Recent commentary has argued that its configuration anticipates sixth-generation fighter shaping. **That commentary is speculation about a classified programme by writers with no access to it**, and this article declines to launder it into a lineage. What can be said is narrower and firmer. **The tailless supersonic fighter did not enter service in the two decades after the MANTA was cancelled**, and the arithmetic above offers one reason why that is unsurprising, which is that the concept as the MANTA stated it fails at the runway rather than in the air.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Four places, and the first is the largest.**

**The ratio treats jet velocity as constant across the envelope and it is not.** A real afterburning turbofan's jet velocity rises with flight speed as ram temperature rises, which would make the supersonic end more favourable than the tables show, and it falls when the afterburner is not lit, which would make the dry-thrust cases less favourable. **The direction of the first error is toward the article's conclusion and the direction of the second is against it**, and neither has been quantified here. The minimum's existence does not depend on the assumption, because it comes from the mass flow term, but its exact location does.

**The engine-out identity assumes the vectoring is available on the live engine at full deflection.** A nozzle that has failed for the same reason the engine has failed provides nothing, and a common-cause failure of an engine and its nozzle is a case a fin covers and a nozzle does not. **This is a reliability argument rather than an aerodynamic one and this article does not make it quantitatively.**

**Treating the two vehicles in one article is a decision about the designation and not about engineering.** They share a contractor, a decade and a number. They share no requirement, no size class, no speed range and no mission. **A reader interested in either aeroplane is being handed a good deal of material about a different one**, and the justification is that the collision itself is the subject.

**The crosswind case assumes the aeroplane must land in a crosswind on a runway.** A vehicle that lands into wind on a long runway at a test range faces a much weaker requirement than an operational fighter does, and the MANTA as an X-plane would have been the former. **The impossibility derived above is a statement about the operational aeroplane the MANTA was a step toward, not necessarily about the demonstrator itself**, and the distinction is real even though every published description of the MANTA frames it as a step toward a fighter.

**The survey below maps the field these two vehicles sit in and is kept separate from the curated sources that carry the argument.** Every record was harvested from Crossref or from the NASA Technical Reports Server, passed through a subject gate written for this article, and assigned to exactly one cluster. **The gate is reported honestly in the Source Base, including the four defects found in it by reading its own output.**

**One statement covers every cluster below and is made once here rather than repeated.** A cluster's size measures how much has been published near a topic and not how important that topic is to these vehicles. The largest named cluster holds unmanned aircraft work that bears on one of the two vehicles and not at all on the other, while the cluster holding this article's keystone, being the tailless configuration itself, ranks ninth.

### Unmanned aircraft, autonomy and the reconnaissance mission

**The largest named cluster, and it bears on one of the two vehicles and not on the other.** Unmanned combat air vehicles, autonomy, reconnaissance and surveillance missions, airworthiness of unmanned systems, and the recent collaborative combat and manned-unmanned teaming work. **Its size is a fact about the last fifteen years of aeronautics and not about the X-44A**, which was flown before most of it was written.

### Engine cycle, installation and inlet integration

**Where the corrected-flow model at the centre of the derivation comes from.** Engine cycle analysis, installed performance, inlet total pressure recovery, afterburning and airframe integration. **The one number this article takes from this body and does not derive is the ram recovery correlation**, and the article shows what its answer looks like with and without it.

### Delta and swept wing aerodynamics at angle of attack

**The wing the MANTA proposed and the flow it would have lived in.** Delta wing vortex aerodynamics, leading-edge behaviour, high angle of attack, post-stall, buffet and flow separation. **A tailless delta at high angle of attack is where the forebody starts generating yawing moments of its own**, which is a mechanism the article names in the framing section and does not quantify.

### Control effectors, allocation and flight control law design

**What replaces a rudder when there is no rudder.** Control allocation for redundant and unconventional effectors, flight control law design for unstable airframes, dynamic inversion, reconfigurable control, and the actuator literature that sets the bandwidth the divergence calculation demands. **This cluster carries much of the recent weight in the survey**, because allocation among many weak effectors is the problem a tailless unmanned aircraft actually has.

### Thrust vectoring and propulsive control

**The mechanism the article's keystone rests on, and it is larger than the problem it solves.** Thrust vectoring has its own propulsion community publishing in its own venues, so it accumulated papers whether or not a tailless aeroplane was being built. The cluster holds nozzle vectoring measurements, multiaxis control power studies, post-stall manoeuvring work, fluidic vectoring, and the flight programmes that carried vectoring hardware for other reasons.

### Nozzles, exhaust systems and internal performance

**The hardware the vectoring has to be built into.** Convergent-divergent nozzle internal performance, thrust coefficients, expansion ratios, ejectors and plug nozzles. **This is the cluster that would decide whether the sidewall yaw flaps the MANTA needed cost more in cruise thrust than they bought in control**, which is a question the article raises and does not answer.

### Tailless configurations and the missing vertical tail

**This is the cluster the article is about and it is the ninth largest, which is a statement about publishing rather than about importance.** It holds the tailless and all-wing stability literature from the 1940s onward, the vertical tail sizing and tail reduction studies, the blended wing body work that inherited the same problem for a different reason, and the modern tailless unmanned configurations. **The oldest records here and the newest ones are asking the same question**, which is how a configuration with no fin is to be kept pointing where it is going.

### Supersonic and transonic aerodynamics

**The speed range in which the article's minimum lives.** Shock waves, wave drag, area ruling, compressibility and the transonic and supersonic characteristics of fighter configurations. **The result that the authority ratio has a minimum near Mach 1.67 is a propulsion result rather than an aerodynamic one**, and this cluster is where the aerodynamic side of the same speed range is recorded.

### What the Shape of the Survey Says

**Three features of the distribution are worth naming.**

**The tailless cluster is smaller than the thrust vectoring cluster, and that ordering is the wrong way round for the subject.** Tailless aircraft are the application and thrust vectoring is one of several mechanisms, so a literature organised around the problem would put the problem first. It does not, because thrust vectoring is a nozzle technology with its own propulsion community publishing in its own venues, and it accumulated papers whether or not any tailless aeroplane was being built.

**The median publication year is 2009 and thirty-nine percent of dated records are from 2015 or later**, which for a subject whose defining flight experiments happened in 1994 and 2001 means the field did not stop when the programmes did. **The unmanned and control-allocation clusters carry most of that recent weight.** The tailless configuration question is being asked again, by a different community, about aeroplanes with no pilot in them.

**Four hundred and fifty-four records predate 1970 and they are not decoration.** The configuration has a documented history running from the 1920s and it is longer than the jet age [[Wooldridge, Winged wonders, the story of the flying wings][book_wooldridge]]. The tailless and all-wing stability literature of the 1940s and 1950s asked the same question with slide rules and free-flight models, and the answer it reached, that the configuration is controllable and the controls have to be unusually powerful and unusually fast, is the answer the 1994 flight experiment reached again with a digital flight control system. **A field that rediscovers its own conclusion fifty years later is telling the reader something about which part of the problem was ever really open.**

## The Source Base

**The argument in this article rests on nine documents and the rest of the reference list is a map of the surrounding literature.** Naming the nine is more useful than characterising the ten thousand.

**Two carry the flight result.** The X-31 quasi-tailless demonstration description [[Huber and Schellenger 1994][research_huberpeter_schellengerharveyg_1994]] and the flight test results report [[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]] supply the flight condition, the technique, the manoeuvres and the conclusion. **Everything this article says about what has actually been demonstrated comes from these two.**

**One carries the nozzle.** The measurement of multiaxis control power from a two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzle with sidewall yaw flaps across Mach 0.20 to 2.47 [[Capone and Bare 1987][research_caponefrancisj_bareeann_1987]] is the evidence that the hardware the MANTA needed can be built and characterised.

**One carries the alternative.** The study of differential canard deflection as a yaw generator on the X-31 with and without its vertical tail [[Whiting 1996][research_whitingmatthewrobert_1996]] establishes that an aerodynamic yaw effector of comparable authority to the vectoring vanes was studied on the same aeroplane, which is what makes the low-speed conclusion above a design choice rather than a dead end.

**Five carry the vehicles themselves and none of them is a primary document.** The MANTA and unmanned X-44A encyclopaedia entries [[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]] [[Lockheed Martin X-44, the unmanned vehicle][ref_x44_uav_wikipedia]], the journalism that broke the story [[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]] [[Skunk Works reveals the missing link in a secret unmanned history][ref_flightglobal_x44a]], and the museum fact sheet [[Lockheed Martin X-44A, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x44a_museum]] are the whole of the public record on these two aircraft. **That is a thin foundation and the article is built to survive it**, which is why the analysis rests on the F-22's published numbers and the X-31's published flight results rather than on anything the X-44 sources say.

**Two sources are used with a stated reservation.** The two National Museum of the United States Air Force pages return a Hypertext Transfer Protocol status of 403 to automated requests, which is bot mitigation rather than absence. **Both were confirmed to exist and to carry the expected titles through search rather than through retrieval**, and neither could be read directly by the tooling used here. Their content enters this article through secondary summaries, and any specification quoted from them should be treated as second-hand.

**The gate had four defects and all four were found by reading its own output rather than by inspecting it.** The pattern for aerofoil was written as a character class that matches the British spelling and a non-word and misses the American spelling entirely, which was caught in the dropped sample on a paper about elastically supported rigid airfoils. The pattern for unmanned aerial vehicles failed on the plural, because there is no word boundary between the final two letters of the abbreviation and the s that follows. Fighter was omitted from the anchor list altogether. The radar-absorbing anchor was written with a space where the literature uses a hyphen. **This is the sixth spelling-variant anchor defect recorded in this series, and every one of them returned a smaller corpus rather than a wrong one, which is why they survive passes.**

**Nine noise families were added to the shared sweep store, in two batches, and the second batch is the more interesting one.** The first five came from reading the sample the gate returned. Cavitating flow in a convergent-divergent nozzle is hydraulics rather than propulsion. The pilot stage of a hydraulic valve is not a person. Biological flight owns the words wing, flight, lift and drag completely. The blended wing body is an underwater vehicle configuration as well as an aircraft one, in the identical phrase. Wind turbine blades are aerofoils and the wind energy literature discusses them in the vocabulary of aerodynamics.

**The remaining four were found by a targeted probe run after the reference set had been built, and none of them appeared in the random sample.** Ship steering owns yaw, roll, rudder and autopilot as completely as flight does. Road vehicle dynamics owns yaw rate control. Civil wind engineering runs wind tunnels and reports crosswind effects on tall buildings and bridge decks. Railway crosswind aerodynamics does the same for trains. **Together they were about half a percent of the corpus**, which is small enough that a sample of thirty was never going to contain one and large enough to be worth removing. **A random sample detects a mis-tuned gate and a targeted probe detects a rare one, and the two are not substitutes.**

**One of those four patterns had to be written carefully and not obviously.** A bare `train` anchor would have removed the scramjet isolator shock train, which is genuinely aerospace, so the railway pattern names the vehicle words instead. A bare `ship` anchor would have removed airships and every use of the word relationship, so the pattern relies on the word boundary that neither of those has. **Each is recorded with the record that produced it**, because a pattern without its incident is a generalisation nobody can later audit.

**All nine were fixed at the gate before any count was written into this article's prose.** That ordering was deliberate. Every survey in this series states its own record counts in prose, so removing citations after the fact desynchronises them, which is the defect class the 2026-08-14 series audit declined to introduce into forty-four finished articles. **Repairing the gate is cheap while the article is still being assembled and expensive afterwards.**

**Two hundred and ninety-six records were refused for not being works at all.** Crossref registers peer reviews as records whose titles read as a review of a named paper, and registers supplementary files as components sharing an identifier stem with their parent. Seventeen further records were military part specifications whose titles are noun phrases inverted for filing, such as flight deck panels, controls and displays. **None of these makes a claim, so none can be a reference.**

**The numerical results are reproducible and were not checked by inspection.** The dynamic pressure identity, the pressure cancellation, the closed form against the atmosphere model, the location of the minimum, the crosswind cancellation, the location of its maximum and the thrust independence of the engine-out angle are each asserted in code, several of them by an independent numerical route, and the assertions are what produced the confidence in them rather than agreement with expectation.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

**The X-44 MANTA was a Lockheed Martin design study of a tailless F-22 derivative controlled by three-axis thrust vectoring.** Preliminary work was under way by May 1999 and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration approved a programme start in June 1999. No aircraft was built.

**The X-44A unmanned aircraft was built by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works in 1999 and first flew in 2001.** It has a span of about 30 feet, is powered by a Williams F112, and was publicly revealed in March 2018. It has been displayed at the National Museum of the United States Air Force since October 2020.

**The X-31 flew a quasi-tailless flight demonstration beginning in March 1994**, at Mach 1.2 and 37,500 feet with a simulated one hundred percent vertical tail reduction, and its report concludes that tailless and reduced-tail fighters are feasible when the capability is designed in from the start.

**The F-22's F119 nozzles vector in pitch only, through plus or minus twenty degrees.**

**The DarkStar was terminated in January 1999 and the Polecat first flew in 2005.**

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**The identity $q = 0.7 p M^{2}$ was checked against the density form at every flight condition used**, agreeing to one part in a million or better.

**The cancellation of static pressure from the authority ratio was checked at five altitudes above the tropopause** and agrees to one part in ten to the twelfth, and the closed form was checked against the full atmosphere model at three further altitudes with exact agreement.

**The minimum of the ideal Mach function at $M = \sqrt{5/2}$ and its value of exactly 1.35 were confirmed by bisection on a numerically differenced derivative**, agreeing to six decimal places, independently of the algebra that produced them.

**The maximum of the crosswind function at exactly Mach one was confirmed by golden-section search** to six decimal places, and the altitude independence was confirmed at five altitudes to four parts in ten thousand, the residue being the small-angle approximation to the arctangent.

**The engine-out relation $\tan \delta = y/\ell$ was confirmed by solving the moment balance numerically without cancelling the thrust**, at four thrusts spanning three orders of magnitude, agreeing to one part in a billion.

### Analysis

**The ratio of thrust-vectored yaw authority to aerodynamic yaw demand is independent of pressure altitude and, above the tropopause, a function of Mach number alone.** This follows from static pressure entering the engine mass flow and the dynamic pressure to the same power.

**That function has a minimum at Mach 1.581 with ideal recovery and Mach 1.674 with a military specification inlet recovery model.** The X-31's demonstrated point at Mach 1.2 stands 1.135 times above the second, and no point from Mach 1.2 to Mach 2.25 is more than twelve percent harder than what was flown.

**For a crosswind of fixed speed, the required vector angle depends on Mach number alone and peaks at exactly Mach one.** Pressure and temperature both cancel.

**Restoring the demonstrated margin on a sea-level approach at 150 knots in a 15 metre per second crosswind requires 38.4 percent throttle against the 7.2 percent the glide slope needs, a factor of 5.33.** The implied lift to drag ratio in level flight at that thrust is between 1.6 and 1.9, which no aeroplane in a landing configuration achieves.

**The directional divergence of a tailless F-22 has a time to double between 0.16 and 0.91 seconds across a wide bracket of the two unpublished quantities it depends on**, and the entire supersonic column of that bracket is inside four tenths of a second.

**A thrust lapse exponent of 0.960 in density ratio reproduces the DarkStar's published ceiling, weight and thrust** on an assumed 42 square metre wing, an Oswald efficiency of 0.85 and a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.015.

### Inference

**The MANTA required a nozzle capability the F-22 does not have**, since a two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzle deflects only in the plane of its flaps. This is inferred from the published nozzle description rather than stated in any MANTA source.

**Pure thrust vectoring cannot meet an operational crosswind landing requirement**, so a tailless fighter needs an aerodynamic yaw effector that works at low speed. This is inferred from the throttle calculation and is consistent with the X-36's split ailerons and with the X-31 differential canard study, neither of which is offered as confirmation.

**The X-44A carries roughly twice the DarkStar's wing loading at a matched ceiling**, which is inferred from an assumed drag polar and aspect ratio common to both. The ratio is far more robust than either loading.

**The X-44A was sized as a configuration and manufacturing demonstrator rather than as an endurance aircraft.** This is inferred from the wing loading and agrees with the stated programme objectives, which were not used in the derivation.

**The stabilisation loop must be machinery and not a pilot**, inferred from the time to double.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the designation X-44A was ever officially assigned to either vehicle, and if to one, to which.** Both are recorded under it in the general reference literature. The specialist designation registry carries no page for the number at all. No allocation document has been published.

**Whether the two programmes had any relationship.** The journalism that revealed the unmanned aircraft states that it is unclear how it came to carry the designation and that there appears to be no direct relation. **An absence of known relation is not a known absence of relation.**

**When the MANTA was cancelled.** Sources give 2000 and 2001 and none cites a programme document.

**Everything about the X-44A's flight programme beyond the year of first flight.** Number of flights, duration, envelope, instrumentation, results, and whether the aircraft in the museum is the only one built.

**Every specification of the MANTA.** Wing area, sweep, weights, required vector angles, control law architecture and the intended sideslip sensing.

**Whether the MANTA influenced any later programme.** Recent commentary asserts a connection to sixth-generation fighter shaping. No evidence for that assertion has been published and this article does not adopt it.

**The DarkStar's wing area**, which is an assumption in this article and not a published figure, and on which the thrust lapse calibration and every absolute number in the X-44A table depend.

### On Sources Used With Reservation

**The two National Museum of the United States Air Force pages could not be retrieved directly**, returning a 403 status to every automated request. Their existence and titles were confirmed by search. **Any figure attributed to them here arrived through a secondary summary.**

**The general encyclopaedia is the source for the MANTA's origin dates, its designation and its F-22 derivation, and for the X-44A's engine, construction material and museum placement.** No primary document for any of those claims has been located. **The article's analysis is deliberately built so that none of its results depends on them**, resting instead on the F-22's published specification and the X-31's published reports.

**Two secondary aviation outlets are cited for the X-44A's revelation and description.** They are the only sources that have published on the aircraft in any detail, they are consistent with each other, and one of them states plainly what it does not know, which is a reason to trust it further rather than less.

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

**This article carries an editorial date of 19 November 2025 and is written from knowledge current at the time of writing**, which includes the 2018 revelation and 2020 museum placement of the X-44A and commentary published after that. **Where later commentary is described, it is described as commentary and not as record.**

## Out of Scope

**Fluidic thrust vectoring**, which replaces mechanical deflection with a secondary injected flow and changes the weight and signature arguments without changing the momentum balance this article rests on.

**The radar cross section calculation itself.** This article takes as given that a vertical tail is a large contributor and does not compute it.

**The X-45, X-46 and X-47 unmanned combat air vehicle programmes**, which are the next articles in this series and which share the tailless configuration question with the X-44A while answering an entirely different requirement.

**Engine-out reliability and the common-cause failure of an engine with its nozzle**, named in the framing section as a case a fin covers and a nozzle does not.

**The manufacturing claim in any quantitative form**, since no mass, lay-up, tooling or cycle-time figure has been released.

**The F-22's own flight control system**, which is a substantial subject and bears on this one only through the nozzle.

## Conclusion

**The X-44 is one number attached to two aeroplanes that share a contractor and nothing else, and the register does not record the collision.**

**The aeroplane that never existed asked a question that had already been answered.** The X-31 flew a fully simulated tailless configuration at Mach 1.2 and 37,500 feet in 1994 and concluded that the configuration is feasible. **What this article adds is how much of the envelope that one point covered**, and the answer, which needs no vehicle data at all, is that the static pressure cancels from the governing ratio, that above the tropopause the ratio depends only on Mach number, that it has a minimum at Mach 1.674 with a realistic inlet, and that the demonstrated point stands thirteen and a half percent above the worst case. **One supersonic point very nearly covered the supersonic envelope.**

**The concept fails at the runway instead.** For a crosswind of fixed speed both pressure and temperature cancel and the demand peaks at exactly Mach one, so at equal throttle the approach is the easiest case in the envelope. **The throttle is not equal.** Restoring the demonstrated margin on approach needs more than five times the thrust the glide slope needs, and absorbing that thrust in level flight implies a lift to drag ratio below two. **A tailless fighter therefore needs an aerodynamic yaw effector at low speed that it does not need supersonically**, which is exactly the architecture the X-36 flew and exactly the architecture the MANTA proposed to delete.

**The engine-out case, which is one of the two reasons fins are large, does not size a thrust-vectored aeroplane at all**, because the vector angle that trims it satisfies $\tan \delta = y/\ell$ and the thrust cancels identically. **Two classic fin-sizing cases, opposite answers, and reasoning from the fin would have got both wrong.**

**The aeroplane that did exist was built in the year its predecessor was cancelled and flew two years later, and almost nothing about it has been released.** Deriving it from its mission puts its wing loading at about twice the DarkStar's at a matched ceiling, which says it was built to demonstrate a configuration and a factory rather than to loiter. **The derivation and the programme's own stated purpose agree, and the derivation did not use the statement.**

**The last observation is about the designation and not about either aeroplane.** The X-planes sequence is a finite resource issued once and never replenished, and a number spent twice is still a number spent once. **The register carries no record of the ambiguity, the specialist directory carries no page for the number, and the encyclopaedia has resolved the collision by writing two articles and noting that they appear to be unrelated.** The cost of the confusion falls entirely on whoever reads the record later, which in this instance is this article.
